rationale: The sibling fixture python/implements-interface-bases proves the `implements` rule FIRES. This one proves it does not fire when the evidence is absent, which is the half a 'does it work' test never covers and the half that keeps a new relationship type from becoming a fabrication. This file imports no interface module at all, and Python does not require one either - a name is a name until something binds it - so `class C(ABC)` here is an ordinary class called ABC and `class D(abc.ABC)` is a base in a module this analyzer has not read. The corpus contains 27 base occurrences of exactly this shape: 24 inside CPython's own typing.py, which DEFINES the class Protocol and then inherits from it, plus asyncio's local `protocols` module. Every one of them is a correct `extends`, and a rule keyed on the spelling rather than on the binding would have relabelled all 27. The file exists to make two guards load-bearing: the root-import condition on a dotted base (mutant M6 deleted it and every python fixture passed, because the only dotted base elsewhere in the suite was abc.ABC, which matches the specific string anyway - a condition nothing tests is not a verified condition), and the shape guard that stops the bare-name proof firing on a DOTTED base (the PY-26 defect). The positive row is deliberate: `collections.abc.Mapping` DOES emit implements here because `import collections` is above and `collections.abc` is the standard library's own namespace, which is the same argument that makes `abc.ABC` self-proving once `abc` is bound. Two dotted bases of identical shape in one file with opposite verdicts, and the only difference is whether the root was bound - that contrast is the test.

expectRelationships.note: the ordinary case: a class base is `extends`, and nothing in this file changes that

`ABC` is undefined in this module. Publishing `implements` would name a symbol the analyzer has never read and that this file does not import. `ABC` is a legal python class name and users define it, which is the whole reason the proof is the binding and not the spelling
same, for the name this lane is most likely to over-credit: 45 proven Protocol bases across the corpus, and 27 unproven ones of this shape
and the most tempting of the three. `Mapping` is the most frequent collections.abc import in the entire corpus, so a spelling-keyed rule would relabel this

THE ROW MUTANT M6 NEEDS. Spelled exactly like a self-proving dotted base, and `abc` is NOT bound in this file - the only import is `collections`. Deleting the root-import condition leaves every other python fixture passing, because the only dotted base the suite held elsewhere was abc.ABC, which matches the specific string anyway and so changed no outcome
the same for `typing`, which is likewise unbound here

THE CONTRAST ROW, and the positive one. `import collections` IS above, and `collections.abc.X` is the standard library's own namespace - there is no plausible user module named `collections` to shadow it, which is the identical argument that makes `abc.ABC` self-proving once `abc` is bound. Two dotted bases of identical shape in this file with OPPOSITE verdicts, differing only in whether the root was bound. This row exists because writing the fixture with `import collections` and then expecting `extends` was wrong and the analyzer was right: a fully qualified stdlib path is a statement about the standard library, not about a name this file happens to have bound

THE BINDING-HONESTY ROW. `VendorProtocol` IS imported by this file - from `vendor.typing`, not from `typing`. Importing a name proves what it was imported FROM; it does not turn it into the stdlib's interface. A rule that recorded imported NAMES without recording which MODULE they came from would relabel this, and would have relabelled CPython's own typing.Protocol subclasses 24 times

forbidRelationships.note: THE FABRICATION THIS FIXTURE EXISTS TO PREVENT. No binding for ABC exists in this file

THE PY-26 DEFECT. In a file that also held `from typing import Protocol`, the bare-name proof fires on a DOTTED base and relabels a third-party class that shares a leaf with the stdlib one. `typing.Protocol` and `vendor.Protocol` share a leaf and nothing else, so every routing decision has to be made on the SHAPE of the base
the M6 behaviour: a dotted spelling is self-proving only once its ROOT is bound
imported, but from `vendor.typing`. Binding the name is not the same as proving the interface
the strongest form of the forbid: `Local` is declared in this very file, so no amount of missing evidence can make it an interface

_seamNote.what: The proof for `implements` is a BINDING, never a spelling. A bare base name is proven only by an import in this file; a dotted base is proven only by a self-proving stdlib spelling whose ROOT this file has bound. `collections.abc.X` is proven by `import collections` alone, because that namespace belongs to the standard library; `abc.ABC` needs `import abc`; `vendor.Protocol` is proven by nothing, however it is imported.
_seamNote.why: A python name is a name until something binds it, and `ABC` and `Protocol` are names users define freely - CPython's own typing.py declares Protocol and then inherits from it 24 times. The 45 proven Protocol bases and the 27 unproven ones are separated by one fact: an import. So the rule keys on the import, and the corpus measurement is what keeps the unproven 27 from being silently promoted by a well-meaning future edit that widens a name set. The dotted root condition is kept because it is the difference between `abc.ABC` proving itself and `someone_elses.ABC` proving itself, and a file that binds neither must see no edge. The one positive row is here to stop the rule from being over-corrected in the other direction: a fully qualified stdlib path IS a statement about the standard library, and refusing it would be refusing a true fact because the surrounding test case was written pessimistically.
